ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a thin square sheet-like conductor, the thickness direction is labeled t, and the side length of the square sheet is labeled L. What is marked by shading/diagonal lines is not the upper and lower large square faces, but the narrow edge faces located on two opposite sides; the size of each shaded narrow edge face is L × t, and the distance between the two shaded faces is the other side length L of the square sheet. Reasoning: The current flows between the two opposite shaded narrow edge faces, and it can be regarded as a uniform conductor, using R = ρℓ/A. Here the current path length ℓ = L, and the cross-sectional area A = L t, so R = ρL/(Lt) = ρ/t. Therefore the resistance does not change with L.

raw_record.question_text: Consider a thin square sheet of side L and thickness t, made of a material of resistivity ρ. How does the resistance between the two opposite shaded faces shown in the figure depend on L?

method.method_draft: First read the figure: the shaded regions are the two opposite narrow edge faces of the thin square slab, not the large square faces. Each shaded face has dimensions L by t, and the separation between the two shaded faces is the other side length of the square sheet, L. From the text, use that the material resistivity is ρ and the sheet has side L and thickness t. Apply the uniform-conductor formula R = ρ ℓ/A with current flowing from one shaded edge face to the opposite shaded edge face. Here ℓ = L and A = L t, so R = ρ L/(L t) = ρ/t. Therefore the resistance has no dependence on L.
